name: Shiatsu

lead: Shiatsu (Japanese for 'finger pressure') is a hands-on bodywork method in which a practitioner presses along the body with thumbs, palms, elbows, knees or feet while the client lies clothed on a mat. It grew out of the older Japanese massage form anma and was shaped into its modern form in the twentieth century.

People use it for relaxation, relief of tight muscles, better sleep and general wellbeing. Via that chain, less tension and better rest and recovery can mean easier training, looser posture and a more rested face. Studies are small and mixed: some report relaxation and short-term pain relief, while reviews describe the evidence base as limited.

paras: Sessions usually last 45 to 60 minutes of hands-on work on a futon or mat, with the client clothed and no oils used. Practitioners combine static pressure, kneading, stretches and joint mobilisation, and some also use abdominal (hara) assessment. Many people book recurring sessions around training or stress periods.

Shiatsu is generally considered safe but can be uncomfortable, and a few adverse events, including a thrombosis and an embolism, have been documented in the literature. Practitioners typically screen for pregnancy, clotting disorders and recent injury. Claims about curing serious disease are not supported by published research.

chain: Sustained finger and palm pressure on muscles

angle.text: People book shiatsu to loosen tight muscles and unwind. Better sleep and recovery can support consistent training and a relaxed, rested appearance. It does not change facial structure.

lead: Shiatsu is a Japanese form of manual therapy whose name means 'finger pressure'. A practitioner applies sustained pressure, stretches and joint mobilisation with the fingers, thumbs, palms, elbows, knees or feet, typically to a clothed client lying on a mat.[1][2]

In appearance terms, shiatsu is used as a relaxation and recovery practice. Proponents describe less muscle tension, easier sleep and a calmer state; for people who care about how they look, those effects connect to better training recovery, looser neck and shoulder posture and a more rested face.[2]

Research on shiatsu consists mostly of small studies. A 2011 systematic review located only a handful of trials and called the evidence preliminary, and some reviews of manual methods list shiatsu among options used for comfort in areas such as labour pain and dementia care.[2][3][4] Traditional explanations based on qi and meridians are not observable phenomena in the view of mainstream science.[1]
infobox: Floor mat or futon; client stays clothed

paras: Practitioners apply pressure with body weight through thumbs, palms, elbows, knees or feet, either holding a point or moving along lines traditionally called meridians. Sessions also include kneading, rocking, tapping, assisted stretches and joint mobilisation.[1][2] Assessment may include palpation, abdominal (hara) diagnosis and sometimes pulse diagnosis.[1]
The Japanese Ministry of Health describes shiatsu as pressure applied without instruments to correct internal malfunctions and promote health.[1]

Shiatsu developed out of anma, a traditional Japanese massage. Under the Tokugawa period anma became associated with blind practitioners, and the Allied occupation's ban on traditional medicine after World War II was lifted after petitions, including one by Helen Keller.[1] The word shiatsu was in use by 1919 when Tamai Tempaku published a book on the finger-pressure method.[1]

Tokujiro Namikoshi founded a shiatsu school in the 1940s and is often credited with the modern form, taught within a Western anatomical framework; his student Shizuto Masunaga added Eastern medical philosophy, leading to Zen Shiatsu.[1][2] Namikoshi is also reported to have helped introduce shiatsu to Western audiences from the 1950s, and Japan recognised it as a separate treatment in 1955.[2]

Practitioners describe shiatsu as balancing the flow of qi through meridians and say it eases back pain, headaches and stress, improves sleep, and supports digestion and circulation.[2] A 1997 nursing article describes it as a deep hands-on treatment that supports general wellbeing.[5]

A 2011 systematic review found only a small number of shiatsu studies and described the evidence as limited, and an Australian government review in 2015 reported no clear evidence of effectiveness for it as a health treatment.[1][2] A later Australian review is reported to rate evidence for musculoskeletal pain as moderate.[2]

Shiatsu is included in broader reviews of non-drug options: a Cochrane review of manual methods for labour pain, an expert review of labour analgesia that lists shiatsu among manual techniques considered safe, and an overview of reviews on sensory stimulation for behavioural symptoms in dementia.[3][4][6] No trial has tested shiatsu for facial appearance.

Shiatsu is generally considered safe though sometimes painful. Case reports include a thrombosis, an embolism and an injury from a shiatsu-type massaging machine.[1] Practitioner guidance includes informed consent and not claiming to treat medical conditions.[2]

timeline.event: Tamai Tempaku publishes a book on the finger-pressure method, using the term shiatsu.[1]
Tokujiro Namikoshi founds his shiatsu college in Tokyo.[1][2]
Japan recognises shiatsu as an independent treatment method, according to one summary.[2]
A systematic review finds the shiatsu research base small and preliminary.[2]
